# Overview {visibility="hidden"}
  


## Survival
  
The objective of survival analysis it to understand the factors influencing mortality rates.
  
Most studies of survival use a "failure time", a.k.a. "time to event" approach.
  
These are continuous-time models in which the random variable of interest is the *survival time* ($T$).
  
There are many great books about survival analysis, and much of the information can be found online. This is a particularly good resource:
  
<center>
[Princeton course](https://grodri.github.io/survival/index)
</center>



## Censoring

Typically, we don't observer survival time for all individuals because some are still alive at the end of the observation period, either because transmitter batteries die or we stop monitoring. 
  
These survival times are "right censored", which means that we know they occurred after the observation window, but we don't know their exact value.
  
There are several types of censoring: 
- Right censoring (common): survival time is in the interval $(U,\infty]$
- Left censoring (rare): survival time is in the interval $[-\infty,L)$
- Interval censoring (rare): survival time is in $(a,b]$. 
    

## Survival
  
There are 4 quantities that you must understand:
  
1. Hazard $\lambda(t)$
    * The instantaneous mortality risk
2. Cummulative hazard $\Lambda(t)$
    * The cummulative mortality risk
3. Survivorship $S(t)$
    * The probability of surviving until time $t$
4. Probability density $p(t)$
    * The relative probability of dying at time $t$
      
  

# Continuous-time models


## Hazard

The continuous-time definition of the hazard rate is the instantaneous mortality risk, conditional on surviving to time $t$:
$$
  \lambda(t) = \lim_{\Delta_t \to 0} \Pr(t \le T < t+\Delta_t | T\ge t)/\Delta_t
$$
  
  
The cumulative hazard can be thought of as the sum of the risks up to time $t$:
$$
  \Lambda(t) = \int_{0}^t \lambda(j) \,\mathrm{d}j
$$


## Survivorship and probability density

Survivorship is the probability of surviving to time $t$ or longer:
$$
%    S(t) = \Pr(T \ge t) = \exp\left(-\int_{0}^t \lambda(j) \,dj\right)
    S(t) = \Pr(T \ge t) = \exp(-\Lambda(t))
$$
  
The probability density is given by the probability of surviving to, and then dying at, time $t$
$$
    p(t) = S(t)\lambda(t) %\exp\left(-\int_{0}^t \lambda(j) \,dj\right)
$$


## Exponential survival times

The simplest survival model is the "exponential model", which assumes that the hazard is constant over time: $\lambda = \lambda(t)$.
  
This implies:
- $S(t) = \exp(-\lambda t)$
- $p(t) = \lambda \exp(-\lambda t)$
  
The mean life expectancy is: $\mu = E(T) = 1/\lambda$. 


##  Exponential survival times -- without covariates

```{r, echo=-1}
#| label: sim0
#| out-width: "60%"
#| fig-align: 'center'
#| fig-width: 9
set.seed(7829)
n <- 100                          ## Sample size
hazard0 <- 1/100
survival.time0 <- rexp(n, hazard0)
hist(survival.time0, xlab="Survival time (time to mortality)", main="")
abline(v=c(mean(survival.time0), 100), col=c("blue", "black"))
legend("topright", legend=c("Sample mean", "Population mean"),
       col=c("blue", "black"), lwd=2)
```




## Exponential survival times

```{r, echo=-1}
#| label: sim1
#| out.width: "50%"
#| fig.align: 'center'
set.seed(7829)
n <- 200                          ## Sample size
x <- rnorm(n)                     ## Covariate
beta0 <- -5; beta1 <- -0.5        ## Hazard coefficients
hazard <- exp(beta0 + beta1*x) 
survival.time <- rexp(n, hazard)
## summary(survival.time)
hist(survival.time, xlab="Survival time (time to mortality)", main="")
```

## Censoring

::: {style='font-size: 80%;'}
Pick a censoring time (duration of study)

```{r}
#| label: cen
ctime <- 500    ## Censoring time
censored <- ifelse(survival.time>ctime, 1, 0)
table(censored) ## Most individuals died before censoring time
```

The observed data, with censoring:
```{r}
#| label: cen1
survival.time.c <- ifelse(censored, ctime, survival.time) 
summary(survival.time.c)
```


:::


## Life lines

```{r}
#| label: life-lines
#| fig-width: 8
#| out-width: '90%'
#| fig-align: 'center'
#| echo: false
plot(0, type="n", xlim=c(0, ctime), ylim=c(1,20),
     xlab="Time", ylab="Individual")
abline(h=1:20, col=gray(0.8))
segments(rep(0, 20), 1:20, survival.time.c[1:20], 1:20)
points(rep(0,20), 1:20, pch=16, col="seagreen3", cex=1)
points(survival.time.c[1:20], 1:20, pch=17,
       col=ifelse(survival.time.c[1:20]==ctime, "blue", "red"))
legend(170, 23, c("mortality", "censoring"), pch=17, col=c("red", "blue"),
       xpd=TRUE, horiz=TRUE)
```



## Kaplan-Meier

Before we fit a model, it can be useful to visualize a non-parametric estimator of the survivorship curve.
  
$$
    \hat{S}(t) = \prod_{j:a_j < t} \left(1 - \frac{d_j}{r_j}\right)
$$

where
- $a_j$ is the time interval
- $d_j$ is the number of mortalities in time interval $j$
- $r_j$ is the number of individuals "at risk" at the beginning of interval $j$
  


## Kaplan-Meier

```{r}
#| label: km
#| out-width: "60%"
#| fig-align: 'center'
library(survival)
y <- Surv(survival.time.c, 1-censored)
plot(y, xlab="Time", ylab="Survivorship", main="Kaplan-Meier")
```

## Parametric survival model

Fit model to simulated data:
```{r}
#| label: survreg
summary(pm1 <- survreg(y ~ x, dist="exponential"))
```


## Estimated hazard

```{r}
#| label: plothaz
#| out-width: "50%"
#| fig-align: 'center'
plot(function(x) exp(beta0 + beta1*x), from=-3, to=3,
     xlab="Covariate", ylab="Hazard", col="black", ylim=c(0, 0.035))
alpha.hat <- coef(pm1)   ## Extract the estimates
plot(function(x) 1/exp(alpha.hat[1] + alpha.hat[2]*x), ## survreg formulation
     from=-3, to=3, col="blue", add=TRUE, lty=2)
legend(0.5, 0.035, c("Estimated hazard", "Hazard"), col=c(4,1), lty=2:1)
```



## Semi-parametric survival model

The Cox proportional hazards model is of the form:
$$
    \lambda_i(t) = \lambda_0(t)\exp(\beta_1 x_{i,1} + \beta_2 x_{i,2} + \cdots)
$$
where $\lambda_0(t)$ is the baseline hazard rate, similar to a Kaplan-Meier hazard.
   
```{r}
#| label: coxreg
(cox1 <- coxph(y ~ x))
```


## Semi-parametric survival model

```{r}
#| label: cox-S
#| out-width: "65%"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-align: 'center'
plot(survfit(cox1, newdata=data.frame(x=c(-2,0,2))),
     xlab="Time", ylab="Survivorship", col=1:3,
     main="Cox proportional hazards fit")
legend(350, 1, paste("x =", c(-2, 0, 2)), lty=1, col=1:3)
```



## Bayesian inference

In JAGS, the recommended way of dealing with censoring is with the `dinterval` distribution. 

[surv-exp.jag](surv-exp.jag)

```{r}
#| size: 'footnotesize'

writeLines(readLines("surv-exp.jag"))
```



```{r}
#| label: load
#| include: false
library(jagsUI)
library(coda)
```



## Bayesian inference
  
Prepare data by treating censored (unobserved) survival times as `NA`. 

```{r}
#| label: jd-surv-exp
survival.time.jags <- survival.time.c
survival.time.jags[censored==1] <- NA
jd.exp <- list(survivalTime=survival.time.jags, censored=censored,
               censorTime=rep(ctime, length(censored)),
               x=x, n=length(censored))
```

Inits, parameters:
```{r}
#| label: ji-jp-exp
ji.exp <- function() list(beta0=rnorm(1), beta1=rnorm(1)) 
jp.exp <- c("beta0", "beta1")
```

Fit the model
```{r}
#| label: js
#| cache: true
#| results: 'hide'
#| eval: true
jags.post.samples.exp <- jags.basic(data=jd.exp, inits=ji.exp,
                                    parameters.to.save=jp.exp,
                                    model.file="surv-exp.jag",
                                    n.chains=3, n.adapt=100, n.burnin=0,
                                    n.iter=2000, parallel=TRUE)
```



## MCMC output

```{r}
#| label: post-samps-exp
#| fig-align: 'center'
#| out-width: '65%'
plot(jags.post.samples.exp)
```




## Posterior hazard

```{r}
#| label: haz-post
#| fig-width: 8
#| out-width: '90%'
#| fig-align: 'center'
#| echo: false
beta.post <- as.matrix(jags.post.samples.exp)[,c("beta0","beta1")]
x.pred <- seq(-3, 3, by=0.2)
lambda.post <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow(beta.post), length(x.pred))
for(i in 1:nrow(beta.post))  lambda.post[i,] <- exp(beta.post[i,1] + beta.post[i,2]*x.pred)
matplot(x.pred, y=t(lambda.post[1:500,]), type="l", col=rgb(0,0,1,0.02),
        xlab="Covariate (x)", ylab="Hazard")
lines(x.pred, colMeans(lambda.post), type="l", col="blue", lwd=2)
plot(function(x) exp(beta0 + beta1*x), from=-3, to=3, col="orange", lwd=2, add=TRUE)
legend(1, 0.06, c("Posterior sample", "Posterior mean", "Actual"),
       col=c(rgb(0,0,1,0.2), "blue", "orange"), lty=1, lwd=c(1,2,2))
```




# Discrete-time models



## Discrete-time survival models

A simple way of modeling survival is to discretize time and use the following model:
$$
    z_{i,t} \sim \mathrm{Bern}(z_{i,t-1}\times \phi_t)
$$

where $z_{i,t}$ indicates if individual $i$ is alive at time $t$ and $\phi$ is the probability of surviving the time interval.
  
  
In discrete time we have:
- Hazard: $\lambda_t = 1-\phi_t = \Pr(t \le T < t+1 | T\ge t)$
- Survivorship: $S_t = \prod_{j=1}^t \phi_j$
- Probability density: $p(t) = S_t \lambda_t$
  


## Simulating discrete-time survival data

Parameters and dimensions

```{r, echo=-1}
#| label: sim-norobust
set.seed(34918)  
maxTime <- 10           ## Time period
n <- 25                 ## nIndividuals
phi <- 0.7              ## Survival probability over 1 time step
```


Generate $z$, the alive-dead indicator

```{r}
#| label: sim-norbust2
z <- matrix(NA, n, maxTime)
first <- rpois(n, 1)+1  ## random release dates
for(i in 1:n) {
    z[i,first[i]] <- 1  ## Known alive at release
    for(t in (first[i]+1):maxTime) {
        z[i,t] <- rbinom(1, 1, z[i,t-1]*phi) ## Alive/dead state
    }
}
```


## Simulated survival data

```{r}
#| label: z
z[1:15,]
```

## Posterior survivorship

```{r, echo=-3}
#| label: phi-post
#| fig-width: 8
#| out-width: '60%'
#| fig-align: 'center'
phi.post <- as.matrix(jags.post.samples.dtime0)[,"phi"]
S.post <- sapply(phi.post, function(x) x^(0:10))
par(mai=c(0.9,0.9,0.1,0.1))
matplot(0:10, S.post[,1:1000], type="l", xlab="Time", ylab="Survivorship",
        col=rgb(0,0.5,1,0.02))
lines(0:10, rowMeans(S.post), col="royalblue", lwd=3)
lines(0:10, phi^(0:10), col="cadetblue", lwd=3)
legend(6, 1, c("Posterior sample", "Posterior mean", "Actual"),
       col=c(rgb(0,0.5,1,0.2), "royalblue", "cadetblue"), lty=1, lwd=c(1,3,3))
```

## Competing risks
  
Competing risks models are used when there are multiple ways of dying, and we're interested in the cause-specific mortality risk, represented by $K$ hazard functions: 
$$
    \lambda_{k,t} = \exp(\beta_{0,k} + \beta_{1,k}x_{t} + \cdots)
$$
  
We can model the conditional probability of dying during interval $t$, with a multinomial link function:
$$
    \pi_{k,t} = \frac{\lambda_{k,t}}{1+\sum_{j=1}^K \lambda_{j,t}}
$$
where the final multinomial cell probability is the probability of surviving: $\pi_{K+1,t} = 1-\sum_{k=1}^K \pi_{k,t}$.
  
The data can be modeled with a categorical distribution:
$$
    z_{i,t} \sim \mathrm{Cat}({\bm \pi}_t | \mathrm{alive\; at\;} t-1)
$$




## Competing risks

Suppose you can die in 3 ways: killed by cougar, bear, or wolf

```{r}
#| label: comp-risk-sim
beta0 <- c(-6, -4, -3) ## log-hazard. No covariates
lambda <- exp(beta0)   ## Cause-specific hazard
pi <- lambda / (1+sum(lambda))
pi[4] <- 1-sum(pi)     ## Probability of surviving t to t+1
```

Set-up the data as a multi-state indicator

```{r}
#| label: comp-risk-sim2
nDeer <- 100
nDays <- 100
z <- matrix(NA, nDeer, nDays)
z[,1] <- 4  ## Everyone starts in state 4 (alive)
```


## Competing risks

There are simpler ways of modeling temporal state dynamics, but we will use a general multi-state transition matrix $\Phi$:
```{r, echo=-3}
#| label: comp-risk-Phi
Phi <- diag(4)
rownames(Phi) <- colnames(Phi) <- c("cougar", "bear", "wolf", "alive")
Phi[4,] <- pi
# kable(Phi, format="latex", digits=3, booktabs=TRUE)
```



------- | ------- | ----- | ----- | -----
       | cougar | bear | wolf | alive
------- | ------- | ----- | ----- | -----
cougar | 1.000      | 0.000 | 0.000 | 0.000
bear   | 0.000      | 1.000 | 0.000 | 0.000
wolf   | 0.000      | 0.000 | 1.000 | 0.000
alive  | 0.002      | 0.017 | 0.047 | 0.934



```{r}
#| label: comp-risk-z
for(i in 1:nDeer) {
    for(t in 2:nDays) {
        z[i,t] <- which(rmultinom(n=1, size=1, prob=Phi[z[i,t-1],])==1)
    }
}
```

## JAGS

Data
```{r}
#| label: jd-comp-risk
Phi.data <- diag(4)
Phi.data[4,] <- NA
jd.comp.risk <- list(z=z, n=nDeer, first=rep(1,nrow(z)), maxTime=ncol(z),
                     nRisks=3, Phi=Phi.data)
```

Initial values
```{r}
#| label: ji-comp-risk
ji.comp.risk <- function() list(beta0=log(runif(3)))
jp.comp.risk <- c("beta0", "pi")
```

Fit the model

```{r}
#| label: js-comp-risk
#| eval: true
jags.ps.comp.risk <- jags.basic(data=jd.comp.risk, inits=ji.comp.risk,
                                parameters.to.save=jp.comp.risk,
                                model.file="surv-dtime-comp-risks.jag",
                                n.chains=3, n.adapt=100, n.burnin=0,
                                n.iter=2000, parallel=TRUE)
```

## Assumptions of failure time models

Random sampling
- Very hard to do in practice
  
Independent survival times
- Problematic for gregarious species
  
Mortality times are known exactly
- Also hard
  
Censoring is random and independent of survival
- This will be a problem if transmitters fail when animals die, and you don't know if they died.
  
Well-defined time origin
- Animals don't have to be released at the same time 
  


## Looking ahead

Most "open population" mark-recapture models use discrete-time survival models, with observation error coming from imperfect detection.
  
Statisticians call these hidden Markov models.
  
Next time, we'll focus on one of the most important examples: the Cormack-Jolly-Seber model.
